questions.rationale: Safety is created by the whole system, including leadership, staffing, equipment, policy and frontline practice.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading a Culture of Safety and Psychological Safety
questions.stem: Which outcome BEST demonstrates effective safety leadership after a reported hazard?

options.text: The report is filed without discussion.
A reminder email is sent once.
The hazard is controlled, staff receive feedback and recurrence is monitored.

questions.rationale: Effective leadership includes action, communication and evaluation of whether risk has actually reduced.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: A medication error occurs after a nurse selects one of two look-alike vials stored together. What is the BEST systems response?

options.text: Separate storage, improve labelling and review selection workflow.
Tell staff to be more careful.

questions.rationale: System redesign addresses the conditions that made the error likely and is stronger than education alone.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: Which factor is an example of a human limitation that safe systems should anticipate?

options.text: Reduced attention during interruptions and fatigue.

questions.rationale: Human factors recognises predictable limits in attention, memory and perception.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: Which intervention is highest in the hierarchy of controls?

options.text: Removing the hazardous product from use.

questions.rationale: Elimination removes the hazard and is stronger than administrative controls or education.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: A unit experiences repeated infusion programming errors. What should the review examine FIRST?

options.text: Only which nurse made each error.
Device design, default settings, workflow, interruptions and training.

questions.rationale: Systems thinking examines interacting human, technical and environmental conditions.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: Which recommendation is MOST likely to produce sustainable risk reduction?

options.text: Standardise concentrations and introduce forcing functions where possible.
Discuss the incident at one meeting.
Ask staff to memorise all doses.

questions.rationale: Standardisation and forcing functions are stronger and more reliable than generic reminders.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of root-cause analysis?

options.text: Understand contributing conditions and prevent recurrence.

questions.rationale: Root-cause approaches seek system learning rather than blame.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: A checklist is introduced but staff frequently bypass it. What should leaders do?

options.text: Examine usability, workflow fit and reasons for workarounds.

questions.rationale: Workarounds are signals that design or workflow may be misaligned with practice.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: Which action best reflects systems thinking?

options.text: Focusing only on the final mistake.
Assuming experienced staff do not err.
Mapping the sequence of events and interacting factors.

questions.rationale: Systems thinking examines the chain of events and surrounding conditions.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: A review finds frequent interruptions during medication preparation. Which control is strongest?

options.text: Redesign the area and workflow to reduce avoidable interruptions.

questions.rationale: Environmental and workflow redesign is stronger than reminders alone.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: Why should frontline staff participate in incident review?

options.text: They understand how work is actually performed.

questions.rationale: Frontline staff provide practical insight into real processes and barriers.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: Which statement about checklists is MOST accurate?

options.text: They support reliable performance when well designed and integrated into workflow.
They are useful only for novice staff.

questions.rationale: Checklists support memory and standardisation but do not replace judgement.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: A technology alert appears so frequently that staff routinely dismiss it. This is an example of:
questions.rationale: Excessive low-value alerts can desensitise staff and reduce response to important warnings.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: Which review question best identifies latent conditions?

options.text: What staffing, interface and workflow conditions made the selection error possible?

questions.rationale: Latent conditions are underlying system weaknesses that shape frontline actions.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: A recommendation is assigned to no one and has no completion date. What is the main problem?

options.text: It is unlikely to be implemented or evaluated.

questions.rationale: Recommendations require ownership, timelines and monitoring to produce change.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: Which control best reduces wrong-patient specimen labelling?

options.text: Bedside barcode verification linked to label printing.
Asking patients to monitor labels alone.

questions.rationale: Engineering and workflow controls reduce reliance on memory and vigilance.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: A team replaces one confusing connector with a non-interchangeable design. This is an example of:

options.text: A forcing function or engineering control.

questions.rationale: Non-interchangeable design physically prevents the wrong connection.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: What is the BEST way to evaluate an incident recommendation?

options.text: Measure whether the targeted risk or event rate decreases.

questions.rationale: Effectiveness should be assessed using relevant process or outcome data.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: Why are 'be more careful' recommendations weak?

options.text: They rely on perfect attention without changing the system.

questions.rationale: Generic vigilance messages do not address predictable human limitations or system design.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: A hospital installs a new device but error rates rise. What should leaders do?

options.text: Assume staff resistance is the only cause.
Review implementation, training, interface design and workflow integration.

questions.rationale: Technology can introduce new risks if implementation and workflow fit are poor.

questions.sectionLabel: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
questions.stem: Which outcome BEST indicates successful human-factors redesign?

options.text: Staff report the process is easier and the targeted error rate falls.

questions.rationale: A successful redesign improves usability and reduces actual risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: A ward wants to reduce catheter-associated urinary tract infections. What should be done FIRST?

options.text: Define the problem and understand current catheter practice.

questions.rationale: Quality improvement begins by clearly defining the problem and understanding current processes.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: Which is an outcome measure for a CAUTI project?

options.text: Percentage of daily catheter reviews completed.

questions.rationale: Outcome measures show what happened to patients or systems, such as infection rates.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: Which is a process measure?

options.text: Percentage of catheters reviewed daily for necessity.

questions.rationale: Process measures show whether recommended care occurred.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: A project reduces infections but causes frequent urgent reinsertion of catheters. Reinsertion rate is a:
questions.rationale: Balancing measures identify unintended consequences of improvement.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: What is the purpose of a small test of change?

options.text: To learn and adapt before wider implementation.
To implement across the whole organisation immediately.

questions.rationale: Small tests allow rapid learning with limited risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: Surveillance data show infections clustering on one shift. What should the team do?

options.text: Explore shift-specific workflow, staffing and practice factors.
Average the data across all shifts.

questions.rationale: Stratified data can reveal local contributing factors that need targeted action.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: Which statement about feedback is MOST accurate?

options.text: Data are useful only when published annually.
Timely, understandable feedback supports local action.
Only leaders need access to results.

questions.rationale: Data support improvement when they reach those who can act in a usable form.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: A hand-hygiene project increases compliance but infection rates do not change. What should the team do?

options.text: Review measurement quality, other infection drivers and implementation fidelity.

questions.rationale: Improvement teams should interpret both process and outcome measures and investigate why expected effects did not occur.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: Which nursing action supports antimicrobial stewardship?

options.text: Administer antimicrobials at the prescribed time and monitor response.
Obtain cultures after antibiotics whenever possible.

questions.rationale: Timely administration, monitoring, culture collection and allergy checking are core nursing contributions.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: Why should unnecessary antimicrobial continuation be questioned through appropriate channels?

options.text: To reduce resistance and avoidable harm.
Because nurses prescribe independently in all settings.

questions.rationale: Unnecessary antimicrobial use increases resistance and adverse effects.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: Which data display would BEST support ward-level action?

options.text: A national report published years later only.
A timely dashboard showing local trends and targets.

questions.rationale: Local, timely and interpretable data are most useful for action.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: A QI project introduces a daily device-review prompt. What should happen NEXT?

options.text: Measure completion, device days, infections and unintended effects.

questions.rationale: Implementation should be followed by evaluation using process, outcome and balancing measures.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: Which statement best defines continuous quality improvement?

options.text: An ongoing cycle of testing, learning and refining care.
A one-time response to serious harm.

questions.rationale: Continuous improvement is iterative and data driven.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: A surveillance system shows rising infections, but case definitions changed. What should leaders do?

options.text: Verify data consistency before concluding performance worsened.

questions.rationale: Reliable interpretation requires consistent definitions and data quality.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: What is the strongest link between infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship?

options.text: Preventing infection reduces the need for antimicrobial treatment.

questions.rationale: Fewer infections mean fewer antimicrobial exposures and less resistance pressure.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: Which project aim is MOST specific?

options.text: Reduce CAUTI by 25% in six months on Ward B.

questions.rationale: A clear, measurable and time-bound aim guides improvement.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: A team collects data but never changes practice. What is missing?

options.text: Translation of findings into tested interventions.

questions.rationale: Measurement alone does not improve care; findings must inform action.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: A nurse obtains a culture using contaminated technique. What is the stewardship risk?

options.text: False results may lead to unnecessary or inappropriate treatment.

questions.rationale: Poor specimen quality can mislead prescribing and promote unnecessary antimicrobial use.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: Which outcome BEST demonstrates successful surveillance use?

options.text: Teams identify a pattern, act on it and observe sustained improvement.

questions.rationale: Surveillance is valuable when it informs action and improves outcomes.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
questions.stem: Why are balancing measures important?

options.text: They are used only for finance.
They eliminate the need for clinical judgement.
They reveal unintended harm or burden caused by an intervention.

questions.rationale: Balancing measures ensure improvement in one area does not create new problems elsewhere.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: An AI deterioration alert identifies a patient as high risk. What remains the nurse's PRIMARY responsibility?

options.text: Use the alert as decision support and assess the patient clinically.
Allow the algorithm to determine care.

questions.rationale: Technology supports but does not replace professional assessment and judgement.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: What is automation bias?

options.text: The tendency to over-trust technology recommendations.

questions.rationale: Automation bias occurs when users rely on automated output despite conflicting clinical evidence.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: A copied electronic note contains outdated information. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Leave it because it was copied from a previous entry.
Verify the patient, correct the record according to policy and communicate significant changes.

questions.rationale: Digital records remain legal clinical documents and require accurate, current information.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: Which action best protects patient confidentiality?

options.text: Discussing patients on personal messaging apps.
Accessing records only for legitimate care purposes and securing screens.

questions.rationale: Information governance requires legitimate access and secure handling of data.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: A remote-monitoring system generates many non-urgent alerts. What is the BEST leadership response?

options.text: Review thresholds, workflow and alert performance with clinical and technical teams.

questions.rationale: Alert fatigue should be addressed through system review and redesign.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: What is the purpose of a downtime plan?

options.text: To guide safe care when digital systems are unavailable.

questions.rationale: Downtime planning supports continuity and safety during technology failure.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates preparedness for an outbreak?

options.text: Developing roles, PPE plans, communication pathways and simulation before the event.

questions.rationale: Preparedness requires planning, practice, role clarity and workforce support before emergencies.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: A disaster plan exists but has never been practised. What is the main risk?

options.text: Staff may not know how to apply it under pressure.

questions.rationale: Plans require rehearsal to identify gaps and build team readiness.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: Which principle is MOST important when sharing a successful intervention internationally?

options.text: Adapt the evidence to local resources, culture and systems.
Assume the same solution fits every setting.

questions.rationale: Global learning should be adapted rather than copied without context.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: A nurse accesses a celebrity patient's record out of curiosity. Which principle is breached?
questions.rationale: Records may be accessed only for legitimate care purposes.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: A wearable device reports normal observations, but the patient looks unwell. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Perform direct assessment and escalate concerns.
Ask the patient to restart the device.

questions.rationale: Clinical assessment overrides false reassurance from technology.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: What is the BEST indicator that digital technology has improved safety?

options.text: Relevant errors or delays decreased without new harms.

questions.rationale: Technology should be evaluated by outcomes and unintended effects, not adoption alone.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: A cyber incident disrupts electronic records. What should nurse leaders prioritise?

options.text: Continuity of safe care, secure downtime procedures and accurate later reconciliation.

questions.rationale: Downtime procedures should preserve care, confidentiality and accurate documentation.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: Which factor is essential for resilient healthcare during emergencies?

options.text: Clear roles, communication, supplies, staff support and continuity plans.

questions.rationale: Resilience depends on coordinated systems and workforce support.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: A hospital shares outbreak data with public-health partners. What is the primary benefit?
questions.rationale: Timely data sharing supports broader surveillance and response.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: Why should nurses report technology-related hazards?

options.text: Digital systems can introduce new forms of patient harm.

questions.rationale: Connected systems may create errors through poor data, design or workflow and require clinical reporting.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: A remote-monitoring program excludes patients without internet access. What should leaders do?

options.text: Develop equitable alternatives such as telephone or community support.
Continue because digital care is efficient.

questions.rationale: Digital innovation should not widen inequity and requires accessible alternatives.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: Which statement best describes global collaboration?

options.text: Exporting one standard solution without adaptation.
Sharing learning while respecting local context and resources.

questions.rationale: Effective global collaboration combines shared evidence with contextual adaptation.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: A digital decision-support tool conflicts with the nurse's assessment. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassess, verify information and escalate using professional judgement.

questions.rationale: Nurses remain accountable for assessment and should investigate conflicts between technology and clinical findings.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: Which outcome BEST demonstrates preparedness and resilience?

options.text: The plan remains unused on a shelf.
The organisation maintains safe essential care during disruption and improves after review.

questions.rationale: Resilience is demonstrated by continuity, adaptation and learning during and after disruption.
